Wald Tests for Environmental Loadings and Dispersion Effects

Source: R/wald_test.R
wald_test.Rd

Wald tests for sets of predictor effects in a fitted rrGDM model:

  • Environmental loadings (lambda): for each predictor, a multivariate (multi-df) Wald test of the null that all free loadings of that predictor (one per latent dimension) are jointly zero. This accounts for the potential covariance between loadings within a predictor. The Size column gives the modulus (Euclidean norm) of the loading vector across the k latent dimensions, a rotation-invariant measure of the predictor's total effect on community composition.

  • Dispersion effects (beta): for each predictor in the dispersion model, a univariate Wald z-test, since each coefficient is a scalar effect on \(\log(\tau)\).

Usage

wald_test(object, include_intercept = FALSE)

Arguments

object

A fitted model of class rrGDM, fitted with se = TRUE.

include_intercept

Logical. Should the intercept term of formula_sd be included in the beta output? Default is FALSE.

Value

A list of class wald_rrGDM with two elements:

  • lambda: a data.frame with one row per predictor in X_design (zero rows if the mean model has no predictors), with columns term, Size, Wald, Df (see Details), Pr_Chisq, Sig.

  • beta: a data.frame with one row per predictor in W_design (excluding the intercept unless include_intercept = TRUE), with columns term, Estimate, SE, z, Pr_z, Sig.

Details

This test is preferred over testing each latent dimension separately (e.g., with per-dimension p-values corrected for multiple comparisons), because it explicitly accounts for the covariance between loadings. If the covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_p\) of a predictor's loadings is singular or ill-conditioned (judged on the correlation scale, so independently of the units of the coefficients; reciprocal condition number below 1e-8), the Wald statistic and p-value for that predictor are set to NA with a warning. This typically indicates unidentified or nearly collinear coefficients, for which the test is not meaningful. If the Hessian at the optimum was not positive definite, the function stops with an error.

The degrees of freedom of the lambda test depend on object$constraint:

  • Under constraint == 1, the loadings matrix is constrained to be lower triangular: predictor (row) p only has free loadings in latent dimensions 1:min(p, k), the remainder being structural zeros that are fixed (not estimated) when the model is fit. The Wald test for predictor p therefore uses Df = min(p, k), and only the free loadings (and their covariance sub-block) enter the test statistic.

  • Under constraint %in% c(0, 2), lambda is unconstrained, so every predictor is tested with Df = k. Note that under constraint == 0 the model is not identified under rotation of the latent space, so individual loadings (and therefore this test) should be interpreted with caution.

See also

anova.rrGDM for tests by variable, summary.rrGDM

Examples

set.seed(2)
# simulate data
n <- 25 # sites
p <- 25 # species

env <- data.frame(temp = rnorm(n), moist = rnorm(n))
eta <- as.matrix(env) %*% matrix(rnorm(2 * p), 2, p)
Y <- matrix(rpois(n * p, exp(1 + 0.8 * eta)), n, p,
            dimnames = list(paste0("site", 1:n), paste0("sp", 1:p)))

# fit model
fit <- rrGDM(Y, env, k = 2,
             formula = ~ temp + moist,
             family = "binomial")
#> ℹ Preparing data
#> ✔ Preparing data ... done
#> 
#> ℹ Finding initial parameters (dbRDA)
#> ✔ Finding initial parameters (dbRDA) ... done
#> 
#> ℹ optimisation
#> ℹ Start 1/1: objective = 1670.1661
#> ℹ optimisation

#> ✔ optimisation ... done
#> 

wald_test(fit)
#> 
#> ── Wald tests: environmental loadings ──
#> 
#>   term   Size    Wald Df Pr_Chisq Sig
#>   temp 0.5957 603.881  1   <1e-06 ***
#>  moist 0.6527 644.000  2   <1e-06 ***
#> ── Wald tests: dispersion effects ──
#> 
#> ℹ No dispersion terms.
#> 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> Wald tests on loadings can be anti-conservative with few samples.
